prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and policy rules, and a microfounded, welfare-based theory of interest rates, prices and monetary policy

statement.case_for: My configuration changed. In round 1 I ranked B047 first and B014 second, and this round I place B014 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. Three of my four round-1 objections to B014 have been answered on substance. (1) I said the trio was unstable because colleagues' opening trios differed. The round-1 files now show that six members arrived at the same three names, and the arguments for it are about the structure of the contributions. Calvo's time-dependent pricing is the primitive on which both the Phillips-curve derivations and the Woodford synthesis rest. Taylor supplied staggered contracts and the policy rule. Woodford supplied the integrated welfare-based theory. Andersson and Fredriksson moved to the trio for exactly that structural reason, which is different from a head count. (2) I worried about saturation from Lucas, Sargent and Sims, Kydland and Prescott, and Bernanke. Hassler and Krusell point out that those prizes went to expectations, time consistency, identification and banking crises, and that none rewarded the pricing friction or the policy rule. I accept that. (3) I raised the framework's failure to anticipate 2008 and 2021-22. Fredriksson is right that the committee rewards originality and lasting influence on how a field analyses its questions, not forecasting success in particular episodes. I should not have treated performance as a merit objection. I keep my fourth objection, that Calvo and Taylor are older contract-pricing and rule insights while Woodford and Gali are the modern synthesis. I now think it is a drafting problem and not a reason to reject the award. On the chair's wording question, a citation that names the specific components (price setting, contracts, rules, the welfare-based synthesis) and does not say 'the New Keynesian framework' makes no claim over the estimated-DSGE tradition of Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets and Wouters. It cannot fully remove the implicit ordering. I think that is an acceptable and honestly stated cost of a three-name cap. On B014 versus B003, my deciding criterion is breadth of influence on both research and the conduct of policy, together with the fact that no prior prize recognised this core. Kiyotaki-Moore has the cleaner attribution, but it has a narrower footprint and a more theory-led record. I regard this as a close call, not a clear one, and I keep both B047 and B003 as serious alternatives.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the main weakness. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler all have strong claims, and the cap leaves them out. Gali is the strongest omitted claimant, and the swap for Calvo is defensible if the committee wants a citation weighted toward the empirical and estimated framework. Calvo's device is compact, and one can ask whether it is a discovery in the sense the committee usually rewards. A specific scientific doubt, from my background knowledge and not verified here, concerns the 2021-23 inflation. If the frequency of price changes rose sharply, that is evidence for state-dependent pricing and against purely time-dependent pricing. It would qualify Calvo's specific mechanism while leaving the case for nominal rigidity as such intact. This is one reason to word the citation around nominal rigidities and not around one pricing rule. Representative-agent versions are also widely seen as being superseded by heterogeneous-agent models, so the prize could be read as honouring a stage of development. Finally, B047 has a cleaner and more broadly tested empirical record, and B003 has the cleaner attribution. I am giving up those advantages and relying on a judgement about breadth of influence.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B030 to B014. He argues that Lucas, Sargent and Sims, Kydland and Prescott, and Bernanke's 2022 prize each covered something different, and that none recognised the pricing-friction and policy-rule framework. He keeps Calvo over Gali because Calvo's 1983 friction is the building block of effectively every New Keynesian model. He invites anyone who reads the post-2021 evidence the other way to state the observation.
responses.response: His distinction answers the saturation worry I raised in round 1, and I withdraw it as an objection to B014. I do not read the post-2021 evidence the other way, but I would note one thing. Evidence on state-dependent price setting during high inflation would bear on Calvo's particular mechanism and not on nominal rigidity in general. That is an argument for wording the citation around nominal rigidities, which I do. He also correctly says that if the committee wants a trade award, B047 is the stronger of the two trade entries. That is consistent with my own round-1 view of Helpman's placement, and I have not moved on it.

responses.point: Krusell argues that Calvo (pricing device), Taylor (contracts and rule) and Woodford (microfounded synthesis) are the most distinct conceptual steps. He regards Gali as the strongest omitted claimant and not a weaker one, and he accepts that excluding Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: In round 1 I said B014 had no stable trio and that this made any citation contestable. His account, and the fact that six files now give the identical trio, undercut that. The structural case for Calvo as the primitive is persuasive to me. I would still not call the cost small, and I agree with him that Gali is the strongest omitted name. I add a disclosure. He and I are frequent co-authors, and my move now coincides with his position. I have tried to rest it on his argument about the primitive and on the answers to my saturation and performance worries, and not on our proximity, but the committee should weigh my view with that in mind.

responses.point: Andersson answered my round-1 file. He would not call monetary macro saturated, and he ranks B047 below B014 because of the Krugman 2008 overlap and the unresolved credit for Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum. He says attribution is not clearly cleaner for B047 once those names are counted. He also says Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans is not derivative, because it concerns identifying monetary shocks and estimating a medium-scale model.
responses.response: His point about B047 is fair, and I raised the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Hopenhayn priority question myself. The two-name agreement among those who ranked B047 is real, but it measures agreement among colleagues, not the cleanness of the underlying priority. I also accept that Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans is a different kind of contribution from the one the citation credits, which I take to be a real cost of the cap. I still disagree slightly on B047. Selection and the extensive margin are a distinct step from Krugman's prize, so I would not rank it low on overlap alone. His arguments move B047 from first to an alternative for me, and they do not demote it much below that.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B003 first. He concedes that B014 has the larger footprint in institutional practice, but says the citation must specify whether it rewards the pricing friction, the policy rule or the integrated framework. He would support B014 if a defensible narrower citation were agreed, and otherwise considers B003 the cleaner prize.
responses.response: The citation I propose names all three components as separable contributions, each tied to one laureate, instead of crediting a single discovery. If that is the meaning of a narrower citation, I think it does meet his condition, although I cannot speak for him. I also accept his distinction between Kiyotaki-Moore's borrower-collateral mechanism and the intermediation and bank-crisis work of the 2022 prize. That is why B003 is an alternative that I take seriously. The difference between us is how to weigh the cleaner attribution of B003 against the broader influence of B014. I do not think that is a question the evidence in the files settles.

responses.point: Enflo keeps B047 first. She treats Melitz as the originator and Helpman as the natural co-recipient, excludes Redding, and thinks the lack of a trade prize since 2008 makes the timing favourable. She acknowledges priority and attribution concerns about Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum.
responses.response: I agree with her on the two-name attribution and on Redding, and on keeping selection and reallocation distinct from Krugman's prize. I would still not count timing in B047's favour, as I said in round 1. Where I now differ is the weight on the open questions. A citation that talks about gains from trade also invites a debate I raised myself, namely how much of the welfare result comes from selection and how much from the model's structural assumptions. That is one reason I would draft a B047 citation narrowly around selection, exporting and foreign investment. I have not changed my view of the science, and I have changed where I place it relative to the other entries.

uncertainties: Whether Calvo or Gali should be the third name, and whether the committee prefers a citation weighted toward the estimated and empirical framework. I would not object strongly to a Gali swap, but I think Calvo is the better choice for a citation built on the primitives.

Whether a citation naming pricing, contracts, rules and the welfare-based synthesis can really avoid implying a ranking against Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler, or whether the cap makes some such implication unavoidable.

Whether evidence from the 2021-23 inflation on state-dependent pricing weakens the case for crediting a time-dependent pricing device specifically. This comes from my background knowledge and I have not verified it.

How much weight prior-prize overlap should carry relative to merit, and whether the committee applies one standard across the 2022 prize (B003), the 2008 trade prize (B047) and the earlier monetary-macro prizes.
Whether my move to B014 reflects the arguments or the influence of close colleagues. I believe it is the arguments, but I cannot rule out bias from proximity to Krusell and Hassler.
My priority and attribution judgements rest on background knowledge of the literature and not on independent verification from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: Updated for this round. The supplied profile lists no co-authorship or institutional link between me and Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair) and an IIES colleague of both, and both prefer B014, which is now my preferred configuration. I have tried to base my move on their arguments and not on that proximity, but readers should weigh it. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, who is credited in B013. That entry is not in my configuration or my alternatives. My research field (growth, firm dynamics, structural change) is adjacent to B047, which is now an alternative, and my profile shows no link to Melitz, Helpman or Redding. The profile weakly suggests, as an inference only, that I may have helped draft the 2025 Scientific Background. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
